paras: The lynching of Tom Roney was the hanging of a Black farm hand by a mob near Woodburn, in Warren County, Kentucky, in the second week of May 1888. Roney was accused of poisoning the horses of a farmer who had discharged him, and he was taken from the house where he lived and hanged from a tree. A Bowling Green wire report carried the story to papers across the country, and one account called it the first hanging in Warren County in many years.

According to a Bowling Green account, J. Marion Sloss, a farmer living about three miles west of Woodburn, lost nineteen horses and mules over the winter and at first blamed disease. When another horse died and two more fell sick, Sloss sent feed from his trough to Drs. Gardner and Duncan, who reported finding a large quantity of poison in it. Tom Roney, described as "of color" and living in the Rich Pond vicinity, had "for a long time" been suspected. The wire report added that he had once worked for Sloss, had been discharged, and had made threats against him.

A mob went to the home of Joe Smith in the Rich Pond neighborhood, where Roney lived, and took him away. The longer account says the men came at midnight on Thursday, carried him to a grove a mile north of Woodburn, and hanged him from the limb of a tree, where his body stayed until it was cut down Friday morning. The wire put the mob at about 100 men, and a Hopkinsville paper described them as masked, but the longer account called it "not a large mob" that worked quickly and "with very little noise." The same account described it as the first hanging in Warren County "for a long term of years."

About two weeks later, Henry Hampton and Jim Lockhart, who were accused of being Roney's accomplices, received letters warning them to leave. Both men went at once to Louisville, leaving their families behind, and the warnings were "supposed to have come from the band that lynched Roney." No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The Bowling Green dispatch of May 11 did not name the victim and ran in papers from Washington and Alexandria to Memphis, Fort Worth and Emporia over the following week. Its headlines differed in emphasis: the Springfield Daily Republic used "Lynch Law in Kentucky," the Evening Star "A Supposed Horse-Poisoner Lynched," and the Waterbury Evening Democrat "A Negro Stock Poisoner Hanged." Copies garbled details along the way, printing the farmer as "Bloss" or "Martin Sloss," the mob as "700 men," and in the Emporia Weekly News the horses as "stolen" under the head "Hanged on Suspicion."

Kentucky papers ran short items that stated the poisoning as fact, and the South Kentuckian called the victim "the scoundrel." The fullest account, printed in the Forrest City Times in Arkansas under the headline "WILL STEAL NO MORE," said nothing had been done earlier because the community did not want to harm Roney "without being sure of his guilt," and called the poisoning "too much for the good citizens of the community." The victim was named only in later items, as Tom Roney in the Forrest City Times and a Big Sandy News follow-up, while briefs printed it as "Tom Honey" and "Tom Rooney" as late as June.

The accounts disagree on when the lynching took place. The wire dated May 11 said Wednesday, which would be May 9, while the longer account placed it at midnight Thursday, with the body found Friday morning, even though that account is itself datelined May 10. The South Kentuckian gave Tuesday night and a Forrest City Times brief gave Friday, and none of these versions comes from clearly better evidence.

reader.title: Lynching of Tom Roney
bases: A mob took Tom Roney from the house where he lived and hanged him from a tree on the accusation that he had poisoned a farmer's horses (A1, A2, A19).

Every account says a mob, given as about 100 men in the wire (A1, A2) or 'not a large mob' locally (A19), hanged Roney without any legal process. The papers give the alleged poisoning of Sloss's horses as the reason (A2, A13, A19).

The Bowling Green wire (A1, A2) and a separate, longer Bowling Green account (A19) agree on the core event, as do the Kentucky briefs (A13, A14) and a later follow-up (A22), though they disagree on the night it happened.

accounts.label: Bowling Green wire (May 11)
accounts.gist: About 100 men took an unnamed negro farm hand from Joe Smith's farm on Wednesday and hanged him; he was 'supposed' to have poisoned Sloss's horses after being discharged, and had threatened Sloss.

accounts.label: Longer Bowling Green account
accounts.gist: Sloss lost nineteen horses and mules over the winter; when another died, physicians found poison in the feed, and a small, quiet mob took Tom Roney from Smith's house at midnight Thursday and hanged him in a grove north of Woodburn.

accounts.label: Kentucky press briefs
accounts.gist: A negro was hanged by a mob in Warren County for poisoning twenty horses; one brief says 100 masked men did it Tuesday night.

accounts.label: Follow-up report
accounts.gist: After the lynching, two men accused as Roney's accomplices received warning letters, supposed to be from the same band, and fled to Louisville.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Bowling Green wire as received under short heads such as 'Lynched.', 'A Negro Lynched.' and 'Colored Farm Hand Lynched', keeping its word 'supposed' about the man's guilt.
The Forrest City Times account called the mob 'good citizens of the community' acting 'systematically and determinedly', and headlined it 'WILL STEAL NO MORE'.
The South Kentuckian stated the poisoning as fact and called the victim 'the scoundrel'.
The Evening Star's head 'A Supposed Horse-Poisoner Lynched' and the Emporia head 'Hanged on Suspicion.' marked the accusation as unproven.

versions.value: Thursday night at midnight, body cut down Friday morning (May 10-11)

conflicts.note: The fullest account is datelined May 10 yet describes the body being cut down 'Friday morning', so its own dates do not agree; the wire dated May 11 says Wednesday. None of the versions is clearly better evidence.
'700' appears in only one copy of the same wire and is probably a misprint of 100.

The 'stolen' variant appears in a reprint of the same wire, and the Forrest City Times headline calls Roney a 'Horse-Thief' over a text about poisoning; the poisoning version is the one in the original wire and the local account.
Variant spellings of the farmer's name; the victim also appears as Tom Roney, 'Tom Honey' and 'Tom Rooney' (A19, A20, A24).

record_check.dossier: May 9 rests on the wire's 'Wednesday'; other accounts give Tuesday night, Thursday midnight (body found Friday morning) and Friday, so the date is uncertain within May 8-11. Nothing supports the record's alternative of 1888-05-17.
